description:
ASTRAVITAL es un equipo apasionado por la ciencia, la tecnología y la exploración espacial. Buscamos desarrollar un software inteligente para monitorear la salud de los astronautas durante sus misiones, detectar riesgos y contribuir a proteger la vida humana en el espacio.

Buscamos personas creativas, comprometidas y con ganas de innovar, especialmente con habilidades en programación, inteligencia artificial, medicina, ingeniería biomédica, análisis de datos y diseño tecnológico.
summary: ASTRAVITAL is a local-first health monitoring prototype for missions to the Moon and Mars, designed to support crews when Earth cannot respond. A browser-emulated smart-glasses interface and Astra, a voice-and-text assistant, explain changes in resting heart rate and left-hip bone density using each astronaut's own reference measurements. A traceable pipeline moves synthetic observations through raw storage, validation and quarantine, normalization, and derived states. The astronaut can repeat a check, inspect its evidence and explicitly save an onboard review request. The full local application includes SQLite storage and an onboard medical officer console; the public web demo provides a browser-only walkthrough and a simulated Earth doctor view. An experimental trend forecast is visible only to the doctor and does not drive alerts. Our contribution connects personal context, understandable explanations and human-controlled review in one workflow. The prototype uses simulated data, not NASA physiological measurements, and does not diagnose or prescribe. Future work targets real sensors, validated models and delayed communications, with potential applications in remote healthcare on Earth.
details:
PURPOSE AND CHALLENGE FIT

ASTRAVITAL helps an astronaut understand a change in their own measurements and choose a next step when immediate support from Earth is unavailable. It responds to "Create Health Monitoring Software for Astronauts on Space Missions" by connecting health indicators, visual self-assessment, explanations and human review. The initial scope is deliberately limited to resting heart rate and periodic left-hip bone mineral density. These two domains demonstrate a shared data and interaction architecture rather than comprehensive physiological monitoring.

THE ASTRONAUT EXPERIENCE

The astronaut enters a browser-emulated glasses view inspired by Snap Spectacles. Heart and Bones status indicators summarize the available measurements. Astra accepts supported questions by text or voice, explains the current comparison in plain language, and exposes the evidence on request. In the seeded walkthrough, Alex Morgan's initial resting reading is 68 bpm. "Check again" produces a repeat of 73 bpm using the original personal reference. The interface then offers preparation of an onboard review request. Saving requires a separate explicit confirmation, and the interface distinguishes a saved request from a delivered message or medical decision.

The optional Body context view links the heart and left hip to their respective summaries. Its anatomy is an AI-generated illustration with visible attribution, not a medical scan, a lesion map or a validated digital twin. Application code renders measurement values, labels and status indicators. The illustration itself is not evidence of an astronaut's condition.

DATA PIPELINE AND PERSONAL CONTEXT

The full local profile uses Node.js and SQLite to retain observations and review state. Incoming records enter Bronze with source and observation metadata. Validation separates unusable or inconsistent records into quarantine with reasons. Compatible records are normalized into Silver before versioned domain rules derive Gold states and their evidence references. Astra queries these structured results rather than executing dictated SQL or inventing physiological readings.

Each astronaut is evaluated against their own eligible historical measurements. The heart rule uses prior valid resting observations and preserves the original reference through a repeat check, preventing an active deviation from being immediately normalized away. WATCH and ALERT settings are simulation parameters, not clinically validated thresholds. Missing, stale, suspect, explicitly faulty and insufficient evidence are treated separately; an unusual value alone does not prove a broken sensor.

The bone workflow compares dated measurements only when region, side, method, units and calibration are compatible. It considers measurement precision and least significant change (LSC). The demonstration uses an explicitly assumed synthetic LSC; unknown precision or incompatible measurements limit the conclusion. A change in density is not a diagnosis of osteoporosis, fracture or porosity, and bone measurements are periodic rather than continuous telemetry.

MEDICAL REVIEW AND COMMUNICATION

The local mission rehearsal includes a crew client, an onboard Crew Medical Officer (CMO) console and an Earth doctor view. The CMO can inspect evidence and record actions without waiting for ground support. Frozen reports enter a simulated Earth queue, and simulated receipt makes them available to the ground view. The configured 3-22 minute one-way delay represents a Mars communication scenario; it is not a lunar delay or a real transport service.

The public web demo opens the same synthetic Alex Morgan case in the glasses and Earth doctor views. Its priority inbox presents confirmed alerts first, and the doctor can inspect heart and bone evidence, switch crew members, magnify the anatomy, acknowledge a case, add a note and record a simulated teleconsult request. Public-demo actions persist in the browser; local-profile actions use SQLite. Neither action storage nor simulated receipt establishes that a real clinician has been contacted or has delivered care.

A unified, explicit message thread between astronaut and doctor is a proposed UX extension. The currently demonstrated interactions are Astra's bounded dialogue, confirmed review requests, report states and recorded medical-review actions.

ADAPTATION, FORECASTING AND CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT

Personalization comes from the astronaut's own reference history. Astra is a bounded, rule-based assistant with fixed response templates grounded in validated data; it is not an unrestricted generative medical chatbot. It declines diagnosis and treatment questions and refers urgent symptom concerns to the onboard medical officer.

A damped-trend Holt forecast is displayed only to the doctor as "Trend forecast · experimental." It uses one usable reading per sol and presents a three-sol horizon with uncertainty. It does not modify alerts or appear in the astronaut's glasses. The repository documents a time-ordered synthetic backtest on 200 crews over 180 sols. That experiment did not establish better performance than repeating the last reading or earlier detection than the existing rule.

The architecture proposes a future release process based on versioned datasets, time-ordered evaluation against simple baselines and current rules, prospective observation and explicit medical approval. This release process is a design direction, not an implemented self-training or autonomous clinical-learning loop. Stored clinician actions provide audit context; they do not automatically become verified outcomes or training labels.

TOOLS AND IMPLEMENTATION

The project uses JavaScript ES modules, HTML, CSS, Three.js for the browser scene, esbuild for bundling, Node.js 22.13 or later, SQLite through node:sqlite, Web Audio APIs and a service worker for cached assets. The full local profile supports whisper.cpp with separately installed pretrained Whisper artifacts for speech recognition and optional Kokoro-82M through kokoro-js and Transformers.js for local speech output. Local-only browser voices or text provide a fallback when appropriate.

The public GitHub Pages walkthrough runs browser-side rules over exported synthetic states. Its browser speech recognition may depend on the browser vendor's online service. The installed local profile is the intended path for operation without a WAN connection after setup, while localhost remains reachable. Native glasses, physical sensors and real Earth transport are not demonstrated by the public link.

ORIGINALITY AND INTENDED BENEFITS

Our contribution is the connection between traceable data processing, a person's own reference, progressive visual explanations and explicit human-controlled review across crew and medical roles. We use NASA resources as design inputs: EIMO motivates onboard capability; Medical Data Architecture informs modular data handling; NASA-STD-3001 informs unavailable-data indications, operator control and explained decision aids. These are design influences, not a claim of NASA certification or endorsement.

The intended benefit is a clearer, locally available path from a changed measurement to informed review. Potential reductions in workload, response time or clinical risk require user studies and clinical evaluation. The same approach could eventually support delayed review in remote terrestrial healthcare.

EVIDENCE, LIMITATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

All physiological observations in the prototype are synthetic, generated reproducibly with seed 142. They are not NASA astronaut records, and generating them does not train the speech recognizer. Repository tests and recorded results document software behavior under specified inputs; they do not establish medical safety, sensitivity, disease prediction or flight readiness. Public browser checks do not substitute for tests of the full local system.

Next steps are real sensor adapters, consent and access-control design for real patient data, validated longitudinal measurements, user testing with crew and clinicians, a bidirectional message experience, real delay-tolerant transport and independently evaluated forecasting. The optional Azure scaffold is not a deployed service. The project remains a software demonstration, not a validated medical device.
